### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Lok Sabha by MP Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi [1], [2]. The bill seeks to establish compulsory registration and regulatory oversight for all computer training institutions across India to prevent commercial exploitation, protect students from exorbitant fees and unapproved closures, and standardise course curricula [2], [3].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor:** Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P. [1].
* **Appropriate Authority:** Appropriate Government (Central Government or State Government as applicable) [3], with rule-making powers delegated to the Central Government [2].
* **Instrument Type:** Private Member's Bill (as-introduced draft, not enacted law) [1], [2].
* **Status / Stage:** Introduced on or after **18 August 2004** [4]; not enacted.

---

### 3. DESIGN & PENAL PROVISIONS
Under **Clause 10** of the Bill, any violation of its provisions stipulates [2]:

| Penalty Component | Statutory Prescription (Clause 10) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Minimum Term of Imprisonment** | **Not less than three years** [2] |
| **Maximum Term of Imprisonment** | **Not in record.** (no upper ceiling specified in the clause) |
| **Fine** | **Not less than one lakh rupees** (₹1,00,000) [2] |

Additional structural requirements in the bill include mandatory prior registration before running a computer centre (Clause 3) [3], an application window within one month of commencement (Clause 4) [3], syllabus and fee determination by the appropriate Government (Clause 7) [5], and mandatory cancellation of registration upon substantiated complaints (Clause 9) [2], [5].

---

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Provides rigorous consumer and student protection against unaccredited, fly-by-night institutes that collect heavy upfront fees without adequate infrastructure or qualified faculty, or abruptly shut down before completing course terms [2].
* **Case Against:** Imposes high criminalisation thresholds for regulatory non-compliance, setting a severe mandatory minimum custodial sentence of at least three years and minimum financial penalties of at least ₹1 lakh without explicit statutory carve-outs or judicial discretion for minor administrative infractions [2].

---

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Legislative Progress:** As a Private Member's Bill, the proposal did not receive official government enactment; check the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship for current executive accreditation frameworks and National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) guidelines.

### 1. WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, a specific fair-dealing exception was proposed to allow lawful users to adapt and copy computer software for operational and debugging purposes without constituting copyright infringement [3][8].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / In-charge:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced in Lok Sabha by Shri Arjun Singh, Minister of Human Resource Development) [11][33].
* **Instrument:** Legislative Bill amending the Copyright Act, 1957 [5].
* **Stage in Record:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha on **6 July 1992** (Bill dated **6 May 1992**) [11][33].

### 3. DESIGN: THE DEBUGGING & ADAPTATION PROVISIONS
The proposal to permit software adaptation for debugging was introduced through two complementary amendments:

1. **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa):**
   * Under **Clause 17** of the Bill, a new **clause (aa)** was inserted into sub-section (1) of **Section 52** of the Copyright Act, 1957 [3][8].
   * The provision exempts from infringement:
     > *"the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
     > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
     > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8].
   * The Notes on Clauses clarify that this amendment was designed to *"cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* [3][7].

2. **Proviso to Section 57(1) (Author's Special Rights):**
   * Under **Clause 20** of the Bill, Section 57 was amended to specify that an author cannot use moral rights to block or penalise such debugging [2][17].
   * It provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies [17].

3. **Exclusion from General Fair Use:**
   * To avoid misuse while protecting bonafide users, the Bill simultaneously amended Section 52(1)(a) to explicitly exclude computer programmes from the general fair-dealing exception for private use/research, channeling permissible software adaptation strictly through proposed clause (aa) [3][8].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Support / Rationale:** Facilitates legitimate software utilisation by enabling lawful users to debug and maintain software utility without facing infringement claims or moral-rights claims from authors [2][3][17].
* **Safeguards / Counter-position:** General private copying exemptions were narrowed for software, and new penal sanctions (proposed section 63C) were added to curb knowing use of infringing computer programme copies [3][13].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Track subsequent statutory enactments (specifically the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994 and 1999) to verify the final enacted numbering and wording of Section 52(1)(aa) and related software interoperability exemptions [4][14].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001 (Bill No. LXX of 2001) is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S.S. Ahluwalia [1, 9]. It seeks to provide free education (from school up to postgraduate, medical, and technical levels), hostels, uniforms, stationery, transportation, and monthly scholarships to the children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were previously engaged in manually carrying human excreta [1, 4].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Chamber / Stage:** Introduced in the Rajya Sabha on **6 November 2001**; Private Member's Bill (as-introduced text) [1, 9].
* **Appropriate Government Defined:** In the case of a State, the Government of that State; in other cases, the Central Government (Clause 2(a)) [1].
* **Rule-Making Authority:** The Central Government is empowered under Clause 9 to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out the purposes of the Bill [6, 9].

### 3. RESPONSIBILITY FOR IDENTIFYING BENEFICIARIES
Under **Clause 3** ("Survey to be conducted by the appropriate Government") of the Bill, the appropriate government is assigned the explicit duty to identify eligible beneficiaries as follows [3, 4]:

1. **Conduct Surveys:** It is the duty of the appropriate government to conduct a survey in the area under its jurisdiction to identify children born of scavenger parents [3, 4].
2. **Prepare Beneficiary Lists:** It must prepare a list of such children who are to be imparted education by the government, in such manner as may be prescribed [3, 4].
3. **Periodic Revision:** It must cause the prepared list of eligible children to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed by rules [3, 4].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS & ENFORCEMENT DESIGN
* **Case For:** Provides targeted universal coverage from primary through technical and medical education to break hereditary occupational bondage and economic distress among families previously engaged in manual scavenging [4, 14].
* **Case Against / Administrative Demands:** Projected a recurring charge of **₹100 crore** per annum and non-recurring expenditure of **₹10 crore** on the Consolidated Fund of India [2, 9]. Furthermore, it creates statutory obligations on scavenger parents to compel attendance (Clause 5) backed by appointed Attendance Authorities (Clause 7) [4, 5].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Prescribed Mechanisms:** Scrutiny rests on whether rules specify the frequency, methodology, and local verification bodies for revising the Clause 3 beneficiary rolls [3, 6].
* **Operational Machinery:** Tracking the notification of Attendance Authorities under Clause 7 who determine whether family economic conditions warrant part-time schooling exceptions under Clause 8 [5, 6].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G.M. Banatwalla, M.P., seeking to provide every citizen the legal right to appropriate work suited to their age, qualification, and strength, or an unemployment allowance of not less than **₹200 per week** until such work is provided [1, 2, 4]. To finance the payment of allowances and related administrative costs, Section 9(1) of the Bill mandates the Central Government to establish a dedicated fund designated as the **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3, 4].

### MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES OF THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1, 3]:

1. **Government Grants:** All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2), which requires the Government to make periodic grants to the Fund as necessary for the purposes of the Act [1, 3].
2. **Voluntary Donations:** All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for rebate or deduction from income-tax under Section 11) [1, 2, 3].
3. **Insurance Contributions:** All contributions in respect of the **Right to Work Insurance Policy** under Section 10 [1, 3].
4. **Beneficiary Contributions:** All sums collected under **Section 12**, which mandates that every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act must contribute to the Fund at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period immediately upon securing employment (whether through the Government or independently) [1, 3, 5].
5. **Investment Returns:** Any interest, dividend, or other return derived from investments made out of any part of the Fund [3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proposer & House:** Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G.M. Banatwalla, M.P. [4].
- **Presidential Recommendation:** Received recommendation from the President under Articles 117(1), 117(3), and 274(1) of the Constitution via Ministry of Labour communication dated **19 April 2002** [6].
- **Legal Stage:** Bill as introduced; it did not receive presidential assent and is not enacted law in force [4, 6].

WHAT IT IS Under the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007) [1, 2], a **"recognised security organisation"** is defined as any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals possessing specific operational qualifications that is authorised by the Central Government via notification in the Official Gazette to perform designated statutory maritime security functions [3, 4]. ### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS * **Governing Statute / Provision:** Section 344K(f) inserted into Part IXB of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 [3, 4, 5]. * **Authorising Authority:** Central Government [3, 4]. * **Mode of Designation:** Official Gazette notification [4]. * **Legislative Stage:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha on **23 December 2004**, passed by the Lok Sabha on **14 August 2007**, passed by the Rajya Sabha on **6 September 2007**, and received Presidential Assent on **24 September 2007** (Act No. 40 of 2007) [1, 2]. ### 3. DESIGN: QUALIFICATIONS & STATUTORY SCOPE To qualify for designation and authorisation by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy substantive competency criteria and be appointed for specific statutory mandates [3, 4]: | Dimension | Statutory Requirement [3, 4] | | :--- | :--- | | **Eligible Forms** | Any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [3]. | | **Core Competencies / Qualifications** | 1. **Expertise** in matters relating to security [3].
2. **Knowledge** of ship and port operations [3]. | | **Statutory Mandate & Scope** | Authorised by notification to carry out:
• Assessment, verification, approval, or certification required under Part IXB of the Act or by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code [4].
• Any security measures on behalf of the Central Government under Section 344M, subject to prescribed conditions [6]. | ### 4. TRADE-OFFS * **Case For:** Enables the Central Government to delegate resource-intensive and technical compliance duties—such as ship verification, security assessments, and port facility compliance under the ISPS Code—to specialized professional bodies, preventing administrative bottlenecks and ensuring compliance so Indian vessels are not barred from foreign ports [1, 4, 6]. * **Case Against:** Outsourcing assessment and verification functions to non-governmental organisations or private corporate bodies requires robust regulatory oversight to avoid conflicts of interest, lapses in security diligence, or variable standards across different private entities. ### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH * **Rule-Making & Gazette Notifications:** Track specific notifications in the Official Gazette authorising recognised security organisations and setting terms under Section 344K(f) and Section 344M [4, 6]. * **Prescribed Standards:** Monitor subordinate rules framed under Section 344T concerning conditions, fees, and delegation of verification and certification duties [6, 7].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 (subsequently enacted as the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005), the statutory framework establishes a legal guarantee of at least **100 days** of wage employment in a financial year to rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work [1], [4]. When wages are linked to output (piece rate), the statutory baseline fixes earnings around a standard daily labour metric [10].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ownership:** Ministry of Rural Development / State Governments and State Employment Guarantee Councils [1], [10].
* **Statutory Authority:** The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 / Act No. 42 of 2005 (received Presidential assent on **5 September 2005**) [7], [8].
* **Status:** Passed by Parliament and enacted into law [7], [8].

### 3. DESIGN: STANDARD WORKDAY DURATION FOR PIECE RATES
When setting piece-rate wage schedules (where wages are directly linked with the quantity of work done), the statute specifies:
* **Workday Duration Standard:** The schedule of rates of wages for unskilled labourers must be fixed such that an adult worker working for **seven hours** would normally earn a wage equal to the statutory wage rate [10].
* **Institutional Mechanism:** The schedule of rates is fixed annually by the **State Government** in consultation with the **State Employment Guarantee Council** [10].
* **Wage Floor Guarantee:** Under no circumstances may labourers be paid less than the specified wage rate [10].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Calibrating piece-rate output norms to a **seven-hour workday** protects manual workers from exploitative productivity quotas, ensuring fair daily minimum wage realization without excessive physical strain [10].
* **Case Against:** Rigid piece-rate schedules based on standard workday hours may lead to implementation friction across diverse terrain, soil conditions, and varying individual worker capabilities, risking measurement disputes at work sites.

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Annual Rate Revisions:** Review State Government gazette notifications fixing the annual Schedule of Rates (SoR) in consultation with State Employment Guarantee Councils [10].
* **Task Measurement:** Monitor Gram Panchayat and Programme Officer compliance ensuring piece-rate measurements allow an average worker to earn the wage rate within a 7-hour work threshold [10].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Bill, 2001**, the interim governance framework provides that the Academic Council of the University of Roorkee continues to discharge its functions during the transitional period until a new Senate is formally established for the Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee [1][2].

### TRANSITIONAL ARRANGEMENT GOVERNING THE ACADEMIC COUNCIL
Clause 6 of the Bill amends Section 38 of the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961 by inserting transitional provisions to ensure administrative and academic continuity upon the conversion of the University of Roorkee [1][2][6]:

- **Continued Functioning**: The Academic Council functioning immediately prior to the commencement of the Act continues to function as such for IIT Roorkee until a new Senate is constituted under the Act [1][2].
- **Cessation of Office**: Upon the constitution of the new Senate under the Act, the members of the Academic Council holding office immediately prior to such constitution cease to hold office [1][2].

### RELATED INTERIM ACADEMIC & STATUTORY PROVISIONS
To support academic and administrative continuity prior to the framing of institute-specific rules, the Bill sets out complementary transitional measures:
- **Interim Statutes and Ordinances**: Until the first Statutes and Ordinances for IIT Roorkee are made under the Act, the Statutes and Ordinances of **IIT Bombay** in force immediately before commencement apply to IIT Roorkee, with necessary modifications and adaptations not inconsistent with the Act [1].
- **Director Assumption**: The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Roorkee is deemed appointed as Director of IIT Roorkee for a period of **three months** or until a regular Director is appointed, whichever is earlier [6][16].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (**TRAI**) issued its consultation paper titled **"Universal Single Number Based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System"** on **15 March 2013** [1]. The initiative was taken *suo-motu* to facilitate the establishment of an efficient and robust Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System (**IECRS**) across India [1].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Authority / Ministry:** Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (**TRAI**), with inputs and coordination involving the **Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)**, the **National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)**, and **State Governments** [1]. Final recommendations were submitted to the **Department of Telecommunications (DoT)** [3].
* **Instrument Stage & Date:** Consultation paper issued on **15 March 2013** [1]; subsequent formal recommendations on *"Single Number based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System (IECRS)"* were forwarded to the Secretary, DoT, on **7 April 2015** [1][3].

### 3. DESIGN
* **Primary Objective:** Establish a unified, single emergency number response infrastructure across India (IECRS) to streamline citizen distress calls to relevant authorities [1][3].
* **Consultation Framework:** The process gathered structured stakeholder inputs and included high-level inter-ministerial deliberations with the MHA, NDMA, and State Governments to structure a pan-India technical and administrative response architecture [1][3].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** A single universal emergency number removes public confusion caused by disparate emergency codes (such as separate lines for police, fire, and medical response) and enables coordinated multi-agency disaster and emergency mitigation [1][3][18].
* **Case Against / Challenges:** Integrating legacy emergency call-handling centers across disparate state jurisdictions requires significant capital outlay, telecom network integration, and technical upgrades to ensure priority routing and location identification without network bottlenecks [2][3].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Tracking Point:** Follow-up policy directives and technical mandate implementation by the **Department of Telecommunications (DoT)** and state-level emergency control room integrations [1][3].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
In its letter dated **19 February 2013** to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI), M/s Unitech Wireless (Tamilnadu) Private Limited informed the Authority of its willingness to extend port-out facilities to subscribers in the **Mumbai** service area following the shutdown of its operations [1, 6]. Because standard SMS-based generation mechanisms were disrupted due to the closure, Unitech requested a special porting mechanism to manually generate Unique Porting Codes (UPCs) after due verification of subscriber details [1].

### 2. PROPOSED SPECIAL CHANNELS
To receive and process subscriber requests for UPC generation in Mumbai, Unitech Wireless proposed three specific touchpoints/channels [1]:
* **Call centre** [1]
* **Company owned company operated (COCO) stores** [1]
* **Authorised direct franchisees** [1]

### 3. TRAI DIRECTION & IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Regulatory Decision:** In its subsequent Direction dated **22 February 2013**, TRAI formally directed Unitech Wireless to accept requests for UPC generation at its **call centres** after subscriber verification, refund remaining account balances within **15 days**, and publish the porting procedure, refund terms, and call centre contact details in newspapers and on its website [2, 3].
* **Action for Other Operators:** All Cellular Mobile Telecom Service (CMTS) and Unified Access Services (UAS) licensees in Mumbai (and Kolkata) along with Mobile Number Portability (MNP) service providers were directed to accept and process these porting requests [2, 8].

### **WHAT IT IS**
In regulatory proceedings concerning Lifecell International Pvt. Ltd. (LIPL)—a private stem cell bank engaged in collecting, processing, and storing umbilical cord blood stem cells—the company was investigated for allegedly misleading promotional representations and contractual liability limitations in its customer agreements [1, 2]. The inquiry originated under the erstwhile Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969 (MRTP Act) before being transferred to the Competition Commission of India (CCI) under Section 66 of the Competition Act, 2002 [2].

### **PROVISIONS ALLEGEDLY VIOLATED**
According to the transfer observations and inquiry record, LIPL was alleged to have contravened the following provisions of the MRTP Act [1, 3]:

* **Unsubstantiated Marketing Claims:**
  * **Provisions:** **Section 36A(1)(i), (ii), (iv), and (vi)** of the MRTP Act (Unfair Trade Practices) [3].
  * **Allegation:** LIPL claimed in its brochures and marketing materials that its *"Lifecell"* service was the *"No. 1 Stem Cell Technology"* and that it was the *"first and only accredited Cord Blood Stem Cell Bank in India"* [1, 3]. Because these claims were viewed as unsubstantiated, the practice was alleged to constitute unfair trade practices under the specified clauses of Section 36A(1) [3].

* **Limited Liability Clauses in Customer Agreements:**
  * **Provisions:** 
    * **Section 2(o)** of the MRTP Act (Restrictive Trade Practices) [3].
    * **Section 36A** of the MRTP Act (Unfair Trade Practices) [1].
  * **Allegation:** The MRTP Commission initially flagged Clause 12 of LIPL's *"Client Enrolment Form and Agreement"*, which limited the company's liability in the event of any loss of specimen, as an unfair trade practice under **Section 36A** [1]. In the transfer observations, it was further alleged that by introducing this limited liability clause, LIPL imposed unjustified costs on customers through the manipulation of service conditions, amounting to a restrictive trade practice under **Section 2(o)** [3].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Enforcing Regulators:** Initiated by the **MRTP Commission** / Director General (Investigation & Registration) [DG(IR)] and subsequently adjudicated by the **Competition Commission of India (CCI)** [2, 3].
* **Outcome:** The CCI ultimately observed that LIPL supported its technological claims with facts and figures (including technical collaboration and testing volume) and had modified the contractual clause; moreover, standard contractual liability limitations common in the industry did not substantiate restrictive or unfair trade practice violations [4, 5].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** was introduced in the Lok Sabha as a Private Member's Bill by **Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P.** [1]. The Bill seeks to regulate computer training institutions across India by mandating prior registration, setting standards for curriculum and fees, establishing a complaints redressal mechanism, and penalizing unauthorized or non-compliant operations to protect students from exorbitant fees, inadequate training, and sudden institutional closures [2, 3].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Category:** Private Member's Bill introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P. (Statement of Objects and Reasons dated **August 18, 2004**) [1, 2].
* **Administrative Authority:** Administered by the **"appropriate Government"** (defined as the **Central Government** or the **State Government**, as the case may be) [3, 4]. Rule-making power is vested in the Central Government [2].
* **Stage & Legal Status:** Introduced bill only (as-introduced version in the Fifty-fifth Year of the Republic of India) [1]. It did not become enacted law.
* **Territorial Extent & Commencement:** Extends to the whole of India; enters into force on such date as the Central Government appoints by notification in the Official Gazette [1].

---

### 3. DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES

| Clause | Provision Summary |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Clause 1** | Short title (*Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Act, 2004*), territorial extent (whole of India), and appointed date commencement by Central Government notification [1]. |
| **Clause 2** | Definitions for **"appropriate Government"** (Central or State Government), **"computer centre"** (institutions conducting courses/advanced courses in computer education, training individuals knowing computer operations, or preparing candidates for IT/related industries), and **"prescribed"** (prescribed by rules) [3, 4]. |
| **Clause 3** | Prohibits any person from running a computer centre without prior registration with the appropriate Government [3]. |
| **Clause 4** | Mandates the in-charge or head of affairs of any existing or new computer centre to apply for registration in the prescribed form within **one month** from commencement [4]. |
| **Clause 5** | Directs the appropriate Government to scrutinize applications, verify the genuineness of centres, and conduct investigations to ensure minimum conditions are fulfilled [4]. |
| **Clause 6** | Authorizes the appropriate Government to issue a registration certificate for such period as it deems fit upon satisfaction [5]. |
| **Clause 7** | Mandates the appropriate Government to prescribe the **syllabus** and **fees** for each course imparted by a computer centre [5]. |
| **Clause 8** | Requires the appropriate Government to investigate any complaint received regarding a centre's functioning and render a decision within **one month** of receipt [5]. |
| **Clause 9** | Requires the appropriate Government to forthwith **cancel registration** if a complaint against a centre is found to be substantiated upon investigation [5, 6]. |
| **Clause 10** | Sets penal provisions for contraventions [6]. |
| **Clause 11** | Empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act via Official Gazette notification [2, 6]. |

---

### 4. PENALTIES
Under **Clause 10**, any person who violates the provisions of the Act faces mandatory minimum statutory penalties [6]:
* **Imprisonment:** Term which **shall not be less than three years** [6].
* **Monetary Fine:** Fine which **shall not be less than one lakh rupees** [2, 6].
* **Administrative Action:** Mandatory and immediate cancellation of registration under Clause 9 upon an adverse finding following an investigation [5, 6].

---

### 5. TRADE-OFFS
* **The Case For:** Addresses consumer fraud in the unaccredited vocational IT education sector where commercial operators charged exorbitant fees, lacked adequate infrastructure or updated course content, and occasionally shut down mid-course, leaving enrolled students stranded [2].
* **The Case Against:** Mandates state-directed fee fixing and curriculum setting (Clause 7) across dynamic, rapidly evolving commercial technology training centres; imposes stringent non-discretionary criminal thresholds (mandatory minimum 3 years' imprisonment and ₹1,00,000 fine under Clause 10) for any statutory violation without differentiation for minor procedural defaults [5, 6].

---

### 6. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Tracking Status:** The instrument was a Private Member's Bill from 2004 (following a prior identical 2001 formulation) and lapsed/did not proceed to enactment; specific subsequent legislative actions on this text are **Not in record.**
* **Regulatory Overlap:** In contemporary skilling architecture, voluntary and statutory accreditation for non-formal IT education and vocational certification operates under bodies like the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) or Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) autonomous bodies (such as NIELIT), rather than a dual-government direct fee/syllabus licensing regime as contemplated here.

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Essential Commodities (Second Amendment) Bill, 1986** was introduced in the Lok Sabha to confer locus standi on aggrieved consumers and recognised voluntary consumer associations to file complaints in court for offences under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 [1, 8, 38, 41]. Prior to this amendment, courts could not take cognizance of offences punishable under the Act except on a written report by a public servant [8, 23, 41].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsoring Minister/Ministry:** Introduced by **H. K. L. Bhagat** (Minister of Parliamentary Affairs and Food and Civil Supplies) [23, 41]. The specific administrative department name is **Not in record** on the Bill sheet itself.
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory amendment Bill (amending Act No. 10 of 1955) [1, 23].
* **Stage & Date:** Introduced in the Lok Sabha with the Statement of Objects and Reasons dated **1st December, 1986** [23, 38]. Passage and assent details for this specific amending bill are **Not in record**.
* **Commencement:** To come into force on such date as the Central Government may appoint by notification in the Official Gazette (Clause 1(2)) [1].

### 3. DESIGN
* **Objectives:** To promote the voluntary consumer movement and facilitate active public and consumer association involvement in enforcing the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 [41].
* **Key Clauses:**
  * **Clause 1:** Provides the short title—*The Essential Commodities (Second Amendment) Act, 1986*—and enables notification-based commencement [1].
  * **Clause 2(a):** Amends **Section 11** of the principal Act to allow courts to take cognizance of an offence not only on a public servant's report, but also on a complaint made by *"any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association, whether such person is a member of that association or not"* [1].
  * **Clause 2(b):** Inserts an **Explanation** defining a *"recognised consumer association"* for the purposes of Section 11 and Section 12AA as *"a voluntary consumer association registered under the Companies Act, 1956 or under any other law for the time being in force"* [44].
  * **Clause 3:** Amends **Section 12AA(1)(e)** of the principal Act, empowering Special Courts to take cognizance of an offence without commit-for-trial not only upon a police report or complaint by an authorized government officer, but also upon a complaint made by *"any person aggrieved or any recognised consumer association"* [38, 44].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Decouples enforcement exclusively from state machinery, empowering citizen-led monitoring against hoarding, black-marketing, and artificial shortages by opening judicial access directly to consumer groups [8, 41].
* **Case Against / Risks:** Expanding direct complainant standing beyond public officials could expose retailers and distributors to frivolous or vexatious private complaints, though the Bill relies on registered consumer bodies to filter claims [41, 44].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Penalties:** **Not in record** (The Bill does not create or amend penalties; it modifies only the cognizance and complaint-filing provisions of Sections 11 and 12AA) [1, 44].
* **Administration:** Administered through the criminal justice apparatus—regular courts under Section 11 and Special Courts established under Section 12AA—alongside Central and State Governments overseeing commodity supply and enforcement [1, 38, 44].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Aircraft (Amendment) Bill, 2006** (enacted as **The Aircraft (Amendment) Act, 2007**, Act No. 44 of 2007) amends the **Aircraft Act, 1934** to align India's civil aviation framework with International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) standards and the Chicago Convention [1, 2, 20]. It broadens Indian jurisdiction over foreign-registered aircraft flying in or over India, expands safety oversight and regulatory powers over air traffic control and navigation systems, mandates investigation of incidents alongside accidents, and significantly escalates statutory penalties to improve regulatory compliance [7, 11, 14, 19].

* **Primary Ministry / Sponsoring Authority:** Central Government (Ministry of Home Affairs); introduced to give effect to the commitment announced in the President's Address on **25 October 1999** [1].
* **Legal Character:** Primary central statute (**Act No. 30 of 2000**) [2].
* **Legislative Trajectory & Stage:** 
  * Passed by the **Lok Sabha on 2 August 2000** [2].
  * Passed by the **Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2000** [2].
  * Amendments made by Rajya Sabha agreed to by **Lok Sabha on 11 August 2000** [2].
  * Received **President's Assent on 25 August 2000** [2].

### 3. DESIGN

#### Key Structural Clauses
* **Territorial Demarcation (Clauses 3–5):** 
  * **Clause 3:** Creates the State of Jharkhand comprising specified territories detached from Bihar, including Bokaro, Chatra, Deoghar, Dhanbad, Dumka, Garhwa, Giridih, Godda, Gumla, Hazaribagh, Kodarma, Lohardaga, Pakur, Palamau, Ranchi, Sahebganj, Singhbhum (East), and Singhbhum (West) [4].
  * **Clause 4:** Designates residuary Bihar as the territories remaining after excluding the districts allocated under Clause 3 [4].
  * **Clause 5:** Amends the First Schedule to the Constitution to list Jharkhand as a State [4, 5].
  * **Clause 6:** Reserves the power of the respective successor State Governments to alter district or territorial boundaries post the appointed day [5].
* **Legislative Representation (Clauses 7–16):**
  * Amends the Fourth Schedule to the Constitution, reducing Bihar's Rajya Sabha seats from **22 to 16** and allocating **6 seats to Jharkhand** [5].
  * Provides for sitting members, representation in the House of the People (Lok Sabha), delimitation of constituencies, Legislative Assemblies, and the Bihar Legislative Council [6].
* **Financial Apportionment (Clauses 40–41):**
  * **Clause 40:** Central revenue shares are distributed between Bihar and Jharkhand by Presidential order based on the recommendations of the Finance Commission under Article 280 [7, 8].
  * **Clause 41:** Apportions assets and liabilities between the successor States based on principles of equity, with the statutory population ratio established as **645.30 : 218.44** (based on the 1991 census) [3, 8].
* **Legal Continuity & Adaptation (Clauses 83–92):**
  * **Clause 84:** Preserves territorial application of laws in force prior to the appointed day until altered by a competent legislature [9].
  * **Clause 85:** Grants the appropriate Government a **two-year window** from the appointed day to adapt and modify existing laws [10].
  * **Clause 91 & 92:** Gives overriding effect to the Act over inconsistent laws, and vests the President with powers to remove difficulties by notified order [11].

#### Penal Provisions
* **Penalties:** **Not in record.** The retrieved text and notes on clauses of The Bihar Reorganisation Bill, 2000 do not contain standalone criminal penal offences or monetary penalty provisions. *(Note: Penal boundary damage provisions retrieved belong to the separate Bihar and Uttar Pradesh Alteration of Boundaries legislation, not this Act)*.

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Arguments / Cases in Favour:** Directly addresses regional self-determination and satisfies the democratic aspirations of the Chota Nagpur and Santhal Parganas populations in Jharkhand [1, 3].
* **Arguments / Structural Burden:** Bifurcated the existing State of Bihar's economic base, separating its primary mineral and industrial resource belts into Jharkhand and necessitating the creation of a dedicated development unit within the Planning Commission under the direct charge of the Deputy Chairman to address the development needs of residuary Bihar [3].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Appointed Day Notification:** Operation of all substantive provisions takes effect from the "appointed day" notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette [12].
* **Statutory Adaptation:** Tracking orders issued by the successor State Governments and Central Government under the two-year statutory clock of Clause 85 for the adaptation/modification of existing laws [10].
* **Asset and Revenue Settlement:** Apportionment of liabilities, state corporate assets, and division of revenues in accordance with Presidential orders and the Finance Commission's Article 280 formula [7, 8].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the **Rajya Sabha** (Bill No. LXX of 2001) by **Shri S.S. Ahluwalia, M.P.** [1, 2, 3]. It aims to break the inter-generational cycle of manual scavenging by obligating the government to provide free, comprehensive educational facilities—spanning from school through post-graduate, medical, and technical education—to children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were previously engaged in manually carrying human excreta [1, 2, 7].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Category:** Private Member's Bill introduced by **Shri S.S. Ahluwalia, M.P.** [3].
* **House of Origin:** **Rajya Sabha** [1].
* **Ministry:** **Not in record.** (Private member's bill).
* **Stage & Status:** As-introduced text (introduced in 2001) [1]. It was not enacted into law.
* **Territorial Extent & Commencement:** Extends to the **whole of India** and was drafted to come into force at once upon enactment [1].

---

### 3. DESIGN

#### Key Definitions (Clause 2)
* **Appropriate Government:** Defined under Clause 2(a) as the **State Government** in the case of a State, and the **Central Government** in other cases [1].
* **Scavenger:** Defined under Clause 2(e) as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the *Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993* [20].
* **Parent:** Includes a guardian and every person having actual custody of the child [20].
* **Attendance Authority:** Authorities appointed under Clause 7 [1, 20].

#### Core Clauses & Provisions
* **Survey & Identification (Clause 3):** Mandates the appropriate Government to conduct surveys within its jurisdiction, prepare a list of children of scavengers to be imparted education, and revise the list at prescribed intervals [22].
* **Educational Facilities (Clause 4):** Mandates the appropriate Government to provide:
  * Free education from school level up to the **post-graduate level**, including higher medical and technical education [24].
  * Free hostel facilities, uniforms, books, stationery, transportation, and other necessary educational assistance [24].
  * Monthly scholarships in deserving cases at prescribed rates [24].
* **Parental Responsibility (Clause 5):** Establishes a statutory duty for scavenger parents/guardians to cause their child to attend an approved school, college, or institution [24, 28].
* **Prohibition on Obstructive Employment (Clause 6):** Prohibits any person from employing a child of a scavenger in any manner that prevents the child from attending school or an educational institution [28].
* **Administration via Attendance Authorities (Clause 7 & 8):**
  * The appropriate Government is empowered to appoint **Attendance Authorities** and assisting staff to carry out the purposes of the Bill [28].
  * If an Attendance Authority determines that family economic or other circumstances prevent regular attendance, it may permit the child to attend an approved part-time institution under specified conditions (Clause 8) [6].
* **Rule-Making Power (Clause 9):** Grants the Central Government power to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette [6].

#### Financial Memorandum
* **Recurring Expenditure:** Estimated at approximately **₹100 crore** per annum from the Consolidated Fund of India [2].
* **Non-Recurring Expenditure:** Estimated at **₹10 crore** [2].

---

### 4. PENALTIES
* **Penalties in Bill:** **Not in record.** The retrieved text of the Bill contains no specific penal clauses, fines, or imprisonment terms for contravention of Clause 6 or other sections.

---

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Administrative Apparatus:** Administration was assigned jointly to the **appropriate Government** (State Governments in States; Central Government elsewhere) for conducting surveys, funding facilities, and appointing **Attendance Authorities** [1, 22, 28].
* **Subsequent Evolution:** While this 2001 private member's bill did not pass into law, subsequent welfare interventions for the children of sanitation workers and manual scavengers have evolved under executive pre-matric scholarship schemes and subsequent statutory frameworks, such as the *Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013* [17].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Prevention of Money-Laundering Bill, 1999** was introduced to establish a comprehensive legal regime in India to prevent money-laundering, confiscate property derived from or involved in money-laundering, and implement international commitments [1, 2]. These commitments stemmed from the United Nations General Assembly Special Session Political Declaration and Global Programme of Action (Resolution S-17/2 of 23 February 1990 and the June 1998 declaration on combating drug-related money-laundering), the 1988 UN Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, and the 40 recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) [2, 3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Legislative History & Stage**: Preceded by the Prevention of Money-laundering Bill, 1998 (introduced in Lok Sabha on **4 August 1998** and examined by the Standing Committee on Finance, which reported on **4 March 1999**) [3]. The 1999 Bill was formulated incorporating those Standing Committee recommendations and was subsequently examined by a Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha (reporting on **24 July 2000**) [1, 3]. The measure was enacted as the **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002** (Act No. 15 of 2003) [2].
- **Ministry Ownership**: The central executive Ministry is **Not in record** in the retrieved legislative synopsis, though administrative authorities are appointed under the central statutory framework.

### DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES

| Chapter / Area | Key Provisions & Clauses | Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Offence Definition** | **Clause / Section 3** | Defines money-laundering: whoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is knowingly a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property [4, 5]. |
| **Attachment & Confiscation** | **Clause / Section 5, 8, 9** | Empowers the Director (or Deputy Director authorized by him) to provisionally attach proceeds of crime for up to **90 days** if there is reason to believe the property may be concealed or transferred [6]; provides for adjudication and confiscation vesting property in the Central Government [7]. |
| **Banking Obligations** | **Clauses / Sections 12–15** | Mandates banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries to maintain and furnish records of transactions under procedures prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India [8]. |
| **Search, Seizure & Arrest** | **Clauses / Sections 16–18** | Empowers the Director and authorized subordinate officers to conduct surveys, search premises/aircraft/vehicles/vessels, seize records and property, and arrest accused persons; searches of females may only be conducted by females [8, 9, 10]. |
| **Evidence & Evidentiary Presumption** | **Clauses / Sections 23–24** | Reverses the burden of proof: accused persons must prove proceeds of crime are untainted property; interconnected transactions are presumed part of money-laundering unless disproved [11]. |

### PENALTIES
- **Primary Offence (Section 4)**: Rigorous imprisonment for not less than **3 years**, extending up to **7 years**, and a fine extending up to **₹5 lakh** [4, 5].
- **Narcotics-Related Predicate Offences**: Where the proceeds of crime relate to offences under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, imprisonment may extend up to **10 years** (and fine up to ₹5 lakh) [4, 5].
- **Reporting Non-Compliance (Section 13)**: The Director is empowered to impose fines on banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries for failing to comply with reporting and record-maintenance requirements [8].

### WHO ADMINISTERS IT
- **Enforcement & Investigation Authorities**: Administered by the **Director**, along with subordinate officers including Deputy Directors and Assistant Directors [6, 12].
- **Adjudicating Authority**: Appointed by the Central Government (under sub-section (1) of Section 6) to adjudicate provisional attachments, interconnected transactions, and confiscations [2, 11, 12].
- **Appellate Forum**: The **Appellate Tribunal** established under Section 25 to hear appeals from orders of the Adjudicating Authority [11, 12].
- **Judicial Trial**: **Special Courts**, designated from Courts of Session under Section 43, to try offences under the legislation [4].

### TRADE-OFFS
- **Strongest Case For**: Equips Indian law enforcement with statutory machinery to track illicit financial flows, attach criminal proceeds before dissipation, fulfill binding international UN/FATF standards, and enforce financial institution transparency [1, 3, 6].
- **Strongest Case Against**: Highly stringent enforcement mechanisms, including reverse burden of proof on the accused (Section 24) [11], extensive search and seizure powers vested directly in administrative directors [9, 10], and rigorous minimum custodial sentences [5].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Commencement**: Enacted as Act No. 15 of 2003 with notification appointed dates determined by the Central Government [2, 12].
- **subsequent Evolution**: Post-enactment amendments in 2005, 2009, and 2012 expanded provisional attachment periods (from 90 to 180 days) [13, 14], broadened reporting definitions to 'reporting entities' [13], and lifted the ₹5 lakh ceiling on criminal fines [13, 15].
